content:
“Coming Out of the Ice” most commonly refers to the memoir by Victor Herman—an American who was trapped in the Soviet Union, spent many years in the Gulag, and eventually returned to the United States—and to the 1982 TV movie adapted from that book.

What it is
- A memoir: Coming Out of the Ice: An Unexpected Life (1979), by Victor Herman with writer William Brashler.
- A TV movie adaptation: Coming Out of the Ice (1982), starring John Savage as Victor Herman.

Who Victor Herman was
- Born in Detroit to Russian émigré parents, Herman moved as a teenager to the USSR in the early 1930s when his father took work helping set up the Ford-linked auto plant in Gorky (now Nizhny Novgorod).
- A gifted athlete and parachutist, Herman set a widely publicized Soviet parachuting/free-fall record as a young man. His visibility—and, by his account, refusal to renounce U.S. citizenship—drew the attention of the NKVD during the late-1930s purges.
- Arrested in 1938, he spent many years in prisons, labor camps, and internal exile in harsh northern and Siberian zones. He describes severe conditions: logging camps, extreme cold, starvation, brutality, prolonged solitary confinement, and the complex prisoner society that developed for survival.
- After serving his sentence, he was confined to internal exile for years. He ultimately secured permission to emigrate and left the Soviet Union in the 1970s, returning to the U.S. with his Russian wife and child.

The book (1979)
- Co-authors: Victor Herman (as told to) with William Brashler.
- Publisher and date: first published in 1979 (Harcourt Brace Jovanovich in the U.S.).
- Content and themes:
  - An American’s-eye view of the Stalinist security state, the Gulag’s mechanics, and post-release “free exile.”
  - Survival strategies: physical endurance, moral compromises, alliances, and moments of humanity among prisoners and even some guards.
  - Identity and citizenship: the cost of maintaining U.S. citizenship in a hostile system versus the pressure to conform.
  - The long tail of repression: how punishment continued after formal sentences through internal exile, restricted movement, and surveillance.
- Style: Direct, testimonial narrative shaped with the help of Brashler; often compared to other Gulag memoirs for its immediacy and detail.
- Reception and impact:
  - Arrived during a period of renewed Western attention to Gulag literature (Solzhenitsyn, Shalamov), but with the unusual vantage of an American caught in the system.
  - Used in human-rights discussions and Cold War-era public discourse about Soviet political repression.
  - Some elements (e.g., exact parachuting records and certain particulars) have been debated, but the broad arc aligns with documented Gulag practices and patterns.

The TV movie (1982)
- Title: Coming Out of the Ice.
- Basis: Adapted from Herman’s memoir.
- Star: John Savage portrays Victor Herman.
- Format: American made-for-television film (network TV in the U.S.).
- Focus: Compresses Herman’s youth in Gorky, arrest, years in camps, and struggle to leave the USSR into a survival drama emphasizing resilience, identity, and the will to live.
- Availability: It has aired on television and circulated sporadically on home video; availability may vary across streaming platforms and regions.

Why it matters
- Unique perspective: One of the few detailed Gulag memoirs by a U.S.-born victim, complementing works by Soviet and Eastern European survivors.
- Historical testimony: Offers granular depictions of camp labor, punishment regimes, prisoner hierarchies, medical care (or lack thereof), climate hazards, and administrative arbitrariness.
- Cultural footprint: The memoir and movie helped bring Gulag experiences to a broader American audience beyond literary circles.

If you’re looking to read or watch it
- The book has seen multiple printings; check libraries, used/rare book sellers, or major online retailers.
- The TV movie may appear on specialty streaming services or be available in DVD back catalogs; searching by title plus “1982 John Savage” often helps.

If you meant a different work with the same or similar title, tell me which medium (book, film, article, etc.) and I’ll adjust.
